title: SYSK Selects: How Breast Implants Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a vintage episode on how breast implants work, curated by Josh. The hosts cover breast implant popularity statistics, the history from Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin's silicone-filled blood bag idea and the Japanese silicone injections after World War Two, to Timmy Jean Lindsay's rose vine tattoo and the first implants, along with silicone versus saline controversy, FDA moratorium and 2006 lifting. Other topics include breast anatomy (lobes, lobules, Cooper's ligament), sizing (ccs, cup sizes, the rice test), shape and texture choices, expandable implants, subglandular, subpectoral and submuscular placement, incision types (periareolar, inframammary, transaxillary, TUBA belly button), related procedures (breast lift, reduction, reconstruction, pec implants, male breast reduction), the polypropylene string implant, and risks like capsular contracture, rippling, bottoming out, hematoma, necrosis, and symmastia. Ends with listener mail about a vulture hitting a windshield.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the SYSK Selects episode and the hosts banter about the show, a disclaimer about breast implants, and a joke about breast size and toilets.

segments.title: Breast implant statistics
segments.summary: The hosts cite rankings of breast augmentation by country, with the US first in total and Brazil, Greece, Italy and Colombia above it per capita, and note breast augmentation overtook liposuction as the top elective surgery in 2012.

segments.title: History of breast implants
segments.summary: Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin developed the early implant after Gerow noticed a plastic blood bag felt like a breast, testing it on a dog named Esmerelda. Earlier, Japanese prostitutes injected silicone, and Timmy Jean Lindsay became one of the first implant recipients after a rose vine tattoo removal. Silicone implants later faced lawsuits against Dow Corning, an FDA moratorium, and a 2006 lifting of restrictions.

segments.title: Breast anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the structural and epithelial components of the breast, including Cooper's ligament, lobes, lobules, alveoli, lactiferous ducts, areola, and the pectoral muscles and rib cage behind the breast.

segments.title: Sizing and the rice test
segments.summary: Breast implant sizes are measured in cubic centimeters and cup size, and the hosts describe the rice test using panty hose filled with rice to estimate size. They also mention that surgeons guide sizing and that size depends on body frame and skin.

segments.title: Implant shape, texture, and expandable implants
segments.summary: The hosts discuss round versus teardrop (contour) shapes, smooth versus textured implants and how scar tissue forms, a researcher's drug-emitting implant concept, and expandable implants filled through a port in the armpit.

segments.title: Placement and incision types
segments.summary: The hosts compare subglandular, subpectoral, and submuscular implant placement, covering recovery, sagging, rippling, and mammogram interference. They then describe periareolar, inframammary fold, transaxillary, and TUBA belly button incisions and their trade-offs.

segments.title: The surgical procedure and plastic surgery
segments.summary: The hosts describe the surgical steps of creating a pocket, positioning the nipple, using sizers, and filling pre-filled implants. They explain the origin of the term plastic surgery and related procedures such as breast reduction, breast lift, reconstruction, pec implants, and male breast reduction.

segments.title: Risks and complications
segments.summary: The hosts list surgical risks including infection, capsular contracture, symmastia, bottoming out, hematoma, seroma, necrosis, mammogram interference, and implant rupture, and mention the polypropylene string implant banned by the FDA in 2001. They also discuss a 2007 study linking implants to suicide that received little follow-up.

segments.title: Sign-off and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts close with a plug for the website and a listener email about a vulture crashing through a truck windshield, followed by contact information.
